title: Social Connections Make People More Likely to Protest
paragraphs: Why do some people join protests while others who share the same views stay at home? According to a major new study, the answer has less to do with personal anger or hardship and more to do with social connections.

The study was carried out by Shelley Boulianne, a professor of communication studies at Mount Royal University in Canada, and Jennifer Earl, a professor of sociology at the University of Delaware in the US. It was published in the journal Science Advances.

The researchers carried out a meta-analysis, a type of study that combines the results of many earlier studies. They examined 181 survey-based studies published between 1965 and 2023, which together included hundreds of thousands of people, mostly in Western democracies. The study focused only on physical protests, such as marches and demonstrations, rather than easier forms of activism like signing petitions or posting online.

The results showed that some factors consistently predicted whether people would take part in protests. These included a strong general interest in politics, left-leaning political views, and membership in groups such as labor unions or community organizations. People who regularly used social media, as well as younger people, people with more education and people living in cities, were also more likely to protest.

On the other hand, personal grievances were not reliable predictors. Factors such as low income, unemployment, dissatisfaction with personal finances and distrust of government did not consistently make people more likely to protest.

Boulianne explained that the consistent predictors are political interest and social connections. Boulianne added that the role of social media is to help people find and maintain these connections. Earl offered simple advice for anyone hoping to encourage participation: specifically invite people to take part.

However, the study has some limitations. Most of the data came from the US and Europe, so the results may not apply to countries where protesting is dangerous. In addition, the data was based on people's own reports, which makes it difficult to prove cause and effect.
